steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on EVE, an efficient vision-language foundation model. Explain the limitations of current architectures and pre-training tasks, describe our model and pre-training approach, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Goal of vision-language pre-training
- Architectures: dual-encoder vs. unified, and their problems
- Pre-training tasks: too many objectives cause problems
- EVE: unified modality-aware Transformer + masked signal modeling
- Architecture details (shared attention, Modality-Aware MoE, modality routing)
- Pre-training task details and results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Goal
  - learn general multimodal representation, transfer to downstream tasks (understanding, image-text retrieval)
  - foundation model: strong performance, easy to train and scale; via architecture and pre-training tasks
- Architectures
  - dual-encoder: modality-specific models (e.g. BERT, ViT) + fusion module
    - shallow fusion (dot product) vs. deep fusion with Transformer Encoders (hard to scale, low efficiency)
  - unified: modality-shared Transformer, simpler, faster, scales; ignores modality gap -> lower performance
  - image: continuous, redundant, low-level; text: discrete, refined, high-level
  - need to consider modality differences
- Pre-training tasks
  - ITC, ITM, Word-Patch Alignment, MLM, MIM
  - more tasks: longer pre-training, more compute, manual loss weighting, less scalability (cf. LLM success)
  - need effective, scalable tasks
- EVE
  - Efficient Vision-languagE foundation model; unified modality-aware Transformer; single task: masked signal modeling
- Architecture
  - shared Multi-Head Self-Attention + Modality-Aware MoE
  - unified shared Transformer: concise, flexible, easy to add modalities, helps cross-modal alignment
  - MoE captures modality differences / modality-specific info
  - modality routing for better expert selection
- Pre-training task
  - unified masked signal modeling = masked pixel + language modeling; faster training, easier scaling
  - other generative methods: extra objectives ITC/ITM, or visual tokens / momentum features (need tokenizer or momentum model)
  - EVE uses raw signals only; 3.5x faster than with ITC and ITM
  - Figure 1: speed; less compute, easy scaling
  - tasks: VQA, visual reasoning, retrieval; SOTA on retrieval and VQA/NLVR2
- Contributions
  - EVE: one unified Transformer, one unified task, SOTA + faster training
  - Modality-Aware MoE in shared Transformer: deeper fusion, modality-specific info, better performance and faster inference
  - unified masked signal modeling: single objective, faster pre-training, competitive performance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Vision-Language Pre-training tries to learn a general multimodal representation that can be transferred to different vision-language downstream tasks, for example vision-language understanding and image-text retrieval. A vision-language foundation model should perform very well and also be easy to train and scale up, and this can be done through the model architecture and the pre-training tasks.

The model architectures of recent methods can be roughly split into two categories, the dual-encoder architecture and the unified architecture. Dual-encoder methods use modality-specific models (e.g. BERT, ViT) to encode the different modalities separately, and then a fusion module to put them together. For the fusion module, some methods use shallow fusion (e.g., dot product) for the interaction between vision and language. Other methods use deep neural networks such as Transformer Encoders to do deep fusion on the modality interaction, but this makes it difficult to scale up and the efficiency is low. Unified methods use a Transformer shared by the modalities to encode them jointly. This makes the framework simpler and faster, and it helps with scaling up the model. However, these methods ignore the gap between the modalities, and so the overall performance is lower. Images are continuous, redundant, and low-level on the raw signals, while text is discrete, refined, and high-level. If a shared Transformer is used directly to encode modalities with a semantic gap, there are problems. So the differences between the modalities need to be considered carefully.

Previous methods have also explored a lot of pre-training tasks for vision-language pre-training, such as Image-Text Contrastive Learning, Image-Text Matching, Word-Patch Alignment, Masked Language Modeling, Masked Image Modeling, and others. They are used widely to improve vision-language pre-training. Adding more pre-training tasks can improve performance, but adding too many tasks also causes some problems. First, it makes the pre-training time much longer and needs more computational resources. Second, the weights for the different objectives have to be adjusted by hand. Third, having too many pre-training objectives can make the model less scalable, and scalability is very important when designing pre-training models, as the recent success of large language models has shown. So we need pre-training tasks that are effective and scalable.

- EVE: Efficient Vision-languagE foundation model; unified modality-aware Transformer; single unified task (masked signal modeling)
- Architecture
  - shared Multi-Head Self-Attention + Modality-Aware MoE, encode and fuse modalities jointly
  - shared Transformer: concise, flexible, easy extension to more modalities, cross-modal alignment
  - MoE: modality differences, modality-specific info; modality routing for expert selection
- Pre-training task
  - masked pixel + language modeling; faster training, easier scaling
  - other generative methods: extra ITC/ITM, or visual tokens / momentum features (tokenizer, momentum model)
  - raw signals only; 3.5x faster than with ITC and ITM
  - Figure 1; VQA, visual reasoning, retrieval; SOTA on retrieval, VQA and NLVR2
- Contributions: EVE; Modality-Aware MoE in shared Transformer; unified masked signal modeling

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Vision-Language Pre-training tries to learn a general multimodal representation that can be transferred to different vision-language downstream tasks, for example vision-language understanding and image-text retrieval. A vision-language foundation model should perform very well and also be easy to train and scale up, and this can be done through the model architecture and the pre-training tasks.

The model architectures of recent methods can be roughly split into two categories, the dual-encoder architecture and the unified architecture. Dual-encoder methods use modality-specific models (e.g. BERT, ViT) to encode the different modalities separately, and then a fusion module to put them together. For the fusion module, some methods use shallow fusion (e.g., dot product) for the interaction between vision and language. Other methods use deep neural networks such as Transformer Encoders to do deep fusion on the modality interaction, but this makes it difficult to scale up and the efficiency is low. Unified methods use a Transformer shared by the modalities to encode them jointly. This makes the framework simpler and faster, and it helps with scaling up the model. However, these methods ignore the gap between the modalities, and so the overall performance is lower. Images are continuous, redundant, and low-level on the raw signals, while text is discrete, refined, and high-level. If a shared Transformer is used directly to encode modalities with a semantic gap, there are problems. So the differences between the modalities need to be considered carefully.

Previous methods have also explored a lot of pre-training tasks for vision-language pre-training, such as Image-Text Contrastive Learning, Image-Text Matching, Word-Patch Alignment, Masked Language Modeling, Masked Image Modeling, and others. They are used widely to improve vision-language pre-training. Adding more pre-training tasks can improve performance, but adding too many tasks also causes some problems. First, it makes the pre-training time much longer and needs more computational resources. Second, the weights for the different objectives have to be adjusted by hand. Third, having too many pre-training objectives can make the model less scalable, and scalability is very important when designing pre-training models, as the recent success of large language models has shown. So we need pre-training tasks that are effective and scalable.

In this paper we propose an Efficient Vision-languagE foundation model (EVE), which has a unified modality-aware Transformer and is pre-trained with a single unified pretraining task, which is masked signal modeling.

For the model architecture, we use a unified modality-aware Transformer and revisit how Mixture-of-Experts can be integrated in vision-language pre-training. The modality-aware Transformer has a shared Multi-Head Self-Attention module and a Modality-Aware MoE module, and it encodes and fuses the different modalities jointly. A unified shared Transformer is more concise and flexible, which makes it simpler to extend to more modalities and helps cross-modal alignment. With MoE, we can take the differences between modalities into account and capture more modality-specific information. We also introduce a modality routing technique in the MoE so that the router can select more appropriate experts for processing.

For the pre-training tasks, we propose a unified masked signal modeling technique that combines masked pixel modeling and masked language modeling, and it greatly improves the training speed and makes scaling less difficult. Some methods have applied the generative pre-training paradigm to vision-language pre-training. But they either add the generative objective together with other complex objectives like ITC and ITM, or they use more complicated targets like visual tokens or momentum features, which need a nontrivial visual tokenizer or a momentum model. All of this makes pre-training more complex. Unlike them, we only use the raw signals from the image-text pairs themselves, to make pre-training as simple as possible and get better scalability. The pre-training speed is 3.5x faster than when ITC and ITM are included.

EVE can make pre-training much faster, as Figure 1 shows. It needs less computational resources and is easy to scale up. We show that EVE is effective on different vision-language downstream tasks, including visual question answering, visual reasoning, and image-text retrieval. EVE gets state-of-the-art performance on Image-Text Retrieval and Vision-Language Understanding (VQA and NLVR2) tasks.

Our contributions are the following:

- We introduce EVE, an efficient vision-language foundation model with one unified multimodal Transformer and one unified pre-training task, which gets state-of-the-art performance and also improves training speed.

- We integrate Modality-Aware MoE with a shared multimodal Transformer to fuse the different modalities more deeply and at the same time capture more modality-specific information, which gives better performance and faster inference speed in a unified architecture.

- We propose a unified masked signal modeling technique that simplifies vision-language pre-training into one unified objective, which gives much faster pre-training and competitive performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Vision-Language Pre-training aims to learn a general multimodal representation that can be transferred to various vision-language downstream tasks, such as vision-language understanding and image-text retrieval. A vision-language foundation model should achieve excellent performance while being easy to train and scale up, which can be achieved through both the model architecture and the pre-training tasks.

The model architectures of recent methods can be roughly divided into two categories: the dual-encoder architecture and the unified architecture. Dual-encoder methods [1,2] use modality-specific models (e.g. BERT [3], ViT [4]) to encode the modalities separately and a fusion module to integrate them. For the fusion module, some methods [1] use shallow fusion (e.g., dot product) for vision-language interaction, while others [2] use deep neural networks, such as Transformer Encoders, to perform deep fusion of the modalities, which makes scaling up difficult and lowers efficiency. Unified methods [5,6] use a modality-shared Transformer to encode the modalities jointly. This simplifies the framework, improves speed, and helps with scaling up the model. However, these methods overlook the inherent gap between modalities, which leads to lower overall performance. Images are continuous, redundant, and low-level on the raw signals, while text is discrete, refined, and high-level. Directly encoding modalities with such a semantic gap using a shared Transformer is problematic, so the differences between modalities must be considered carefully.

Previous methods have also explored many pre-training tasks for vision-language pre-training, including Image-Text Contrastive Learning [1], Image-Text Matching [7], Word-Patch Alignment [8], Masked Language Modeling [9], Masked Image Modeling [10], and so on, and these tasks have been widely used to improve vision-language pre-training. While more pre-training tasks can enhance performance, too many tasks also lead to problems. First, they significantly prolong pre-training and increase the computational resources required. Second, they require manual weight adjustments for the different objectives. Third, too many pre-training objectives can reduce the model's scalability, which is crucial in designing pre-training models, as the recent success of large language models has shown [11,12,13]. Effective and scalable pre-training tasks are therefore necessary.

In this paper, we propose an Efficient Vision-languagE foundation model (EVE) with a unified modality-aware Transformer, pre-trained with a single unified pretraining task, i.e., masked signal modeling.

In terms of model architecture, we use a unified modality-aware Transformer and revisit the integration of Mixture-of-Experts in vision-language pre-training. The modality-aware Transformer uses a shared Multi-Head Self-Attention module and a Modality-Aware MoE module to encode and fuse the modalities jointly. A unified shared Transformer is more concise and flexible, which simplifies extension to additional modalities and facilitates cross-modal alignment. By incorporating MoE, we can account for the differences between modalities and capture more modality-specific information. We also introduce a modality routing technique in MoE that lets the router select more appropriate experts for processing.

In terms of pre-training tasks, we propose a unified masked signal modeling technique that combines masked pixel and language modeling, significantly improving training speed and reducing scaling difficulty. Some methods [14,15,16] have applied the generative pre-training paradigm to vision-language pre-training. However, they either combine the generative objective with other complex objectives like ITC and ITM [15] or use more complicated targets such as visual tokens [14] or momentum features [16], which require a nontrivial visual tokenizer or momentum model. All of these add complexity to pre-training. In contrast, we use only the raw signals from the image-text pairs themselves to minimize pre-training complexity and achieve better scalability. Pre-training is 3.5x faster than when ITC and ITM are incorporated.

As shown in Figure 1, EVE greatly increases pre-training speed, reducing the demand for extensive computational resources while remaining easy to scale up. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EVE on various vision-language downstream tasks, including visual question answering, visual reasoning, and image-text retrieval, where EVE achieves state-of-the-art performance on Image-Text Retrieval and Vision-Language Understanding (VQA and NLVR2) tasks.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- We introduce EVE, an efficient vision-language foundation model with one unified multimodal Transformer and one unified pre-training task, which achieves state-of-the-art performance while improving training speed.

- We integrate Modality-Aware MoE with a shared multimodal Transformer to achieve deeper fusion of the modalities while also capturing more modality-specific information, which results in better performance and faster inference within a unified architecture.

- We propose a unified masked signal modeling technique that simplifies vision-language pre-training into a single unified objective, resulting in significantly faster pre-training and competitive performance.
